title: Explicit dense robust graphs with efficient local self-ordering
formal: Historical construction question, resolved affirmatively: construct an infinite family of simple undirected graphs G_n=([n],E_n) with Ω(n) robust self-ordering and an efficient local procedure that recovers the canonical name of any vertex in an arbitrary relabelled copy. More precisely, the family has an absolute γ>0 such that |E_n△π(E_n)|≥γn·|{v:π(v)≠v}| for every vertex permutation π, together with a uniform randomized adjacency-query algorithm that recovers the canonical name of a requested vertex with probability at least 2/3 using poly(log n) time. Corollary 1.7 of Goldreich’s checked revision supplies this family and additionally computes its own adjacency predicate in deterministic poly(log n) time, meeting the source’s efficient-construction requirement.
context:
An asymmetric graph gives every vertex a unique identity determined by the full graph. Local self-ordering asks whether that identity can be recovered from a small number of adjacency queries. Robust self-ordering separately requires every nontrivial relabelling to change many edges.

The saved excerpt began with a probability-distribution sentence from footnote 44. The actual open question is footnote 45: an efficient construction of dense, linearly robust graphs supporting local self-ordering. The source already distinguished this from information-theoretic existence.

Goldreich’s Theorem 1.6 preserves linear robustness while producing graphs with polylogarithmic-time local self-ordering. Corollary 1.7 states the resulting explicit family and also gives a polylogarithmic-time canonical adjacency predicate. These are the simultaneous guarantees missing from the original paragraph.

The same revision lists as Problem 1.5 whether every linearly robust dense graph has a polylogarithmic-query local procedure. Constructing one family with both properties answers this card, without establishing that universal implication.
why: Provides efficiently accessible canonical vertex identities in dense graphs while retaining strong asymmetry, enabling explicit constructions in graph property testing.

references.title: Robustly Self-Ordered Graphs: Constructions and Applications to Property Testing
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 64; PDF page 64

definitions: A simple undirected graph has vertex set [n]={1,…,n} and an edge set E_n of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. For a permutation π of [n], π(E_n)={{π(u),π(v)}:{u,v}∈E_n}. The symmetric difference A△B consists of elements belonging to exactly one of A,B, so the robustness inequality counts changed unordered edges. A graph is self-ordered if its only automorphism is the identity; positive robustness implies this. Given a graph H=([n],F) isomorphic to G_n, there is therefore a unique bijection φ:[n]→[n] satisfying {u,v}∈F iff {φ(u),φ(v)}∈E_n. The local algorithm receives n and a vertex v of H in binary, can query whether any pair is adjacent in H, and must output φ(v). Correctness is required for each H and each v separately, with probability over its internal coins. It is promised an exact isomorphic copy, not a graph with adversarial edge corruptions. Queries are adaptive and each answer is one bit; the polylogarithmic running time counts ordinary computation as well as oracle calls. The family’s canonical adjacency algorithm receives (n,u,v) in binary and decides {u,v}∈E_n. Uniform means fixed algorithms across the family, with no n-dependent advice; poly(log n) means C(log₂(n+1))^a for constants C,a independent of n,H,v. The statement concerns the asymptotic infinite family asserted by the construction; finitely many small sizes do not affect its guarantees. The oracle is the adjacency predicate of a dense graph, not an oracle listing a selected neighbor.
answer_criterion: The affirmative resolution must simultaneously supply the robust graph family, its efficient construction and a polylogarithmic-time local self-ordering algorithm under arbitrary relabelling. The cited Corollary 1.7 provides these guarantees. Mere existence of graphs with few-query but computationally unbounded recovery, or a polynomial-time algorithm reading the full graph, would not have answered the source question.
